1.pericope_label: Moreover, when ye shall divide by lot the land for inheritance, ye shall offer an oblation unto the Lord, an holy portion of the land: the length shall be the length of five and twenty thousand reeds, and the breadth shall be ten thousand. This shall be holy in all the borders thereof round about. Of this there shall be for the sanctuary five hundred in length, with five hundred in breadth, square round about; and fifty cubits round about for the suburbs thereof. And of this measure shalt thou measure the length of five and twenty thousand, and the breadth of ten thousand: and in it shall be the sanctuary and the most holy place. The holy portion of the land shall be for the priests the ministers of the sanctuary, which shall come near to minister unto the Lord: and it shall be a place for their houses, and an holy place for the sanctuary. And the five and twenty thousand of length, and the ten thousand of breadth, shall also the Levites, the ministers of the house, have for themselves, for a possession for twenty chambers. And ye shall appoint the possession of the city five thousand broad, and five and twenty thousand long, over against the oblation of the holy portion: it shall be for the whole house of Israel. And a portion shall be for the prince on the one side and on the other side of the oblation of the holy portion, and of the possession of the city, before the oblation of the holy portion, and before the possession of the city, from the west side westward, and from the east side eastward: and the length shall be over against one of the portions, from the west border unto the east border. In the land shall be his possession in Israel: and my princes shall no more oppress my people; and the rest of the land shall they give to the house of Israel according to their tribes.

schools.summary: Ellicott works the measurements out in detail: dividing by lot implies no chance, since each tribe is later named; the unspoken unit must be reeds, making the oblation over forty-seven miles long; the Greek variant for the breadth is declined as no improvement; the priests' territory is enormously larger than the older law's provision, which he explains by proportion to the enlarged sanctuary rather than as a substitute for tithes; a corrupt clause in the Levites' portion he mends by transposing letters to read a possession of gates to dwell in; and he denies that the city here is Jerusalem at all. Keil and Delitzsch print the disputed breadth with a query.

Gill denies that any literal division is meant -- not the conquest, not the return from Babylon, not the latter-day conversion, and not even a type of heaven -- and reads the whole allotment as the settling of Christ's kingdom through the world; the city he takes for the civil state of God's people under the spiritual reign, and the prince for the Messiah rather than any magistrate.

Clarke keeps the passage on the ground: each family resettles by its former allotment, the land was not divided afresh by lot after the captivity, and what is described is only the provision for temple, priests and prince. He glosses the prince as the chief magistrate and names the old oppression as exorbitant taxes for profligate courts and subsidies paid out of the temple. Wesley reckons the whole survey in cubits rather than reeds and takes the city for the capital.

Henry holds that the division was never accomplished in the Jewish state and finds it fulfilled in the Christian church, as new as this scheme is unlike the old one; from the measuring of the holy portion he draws the lesson that its borders were fixed so the sanctuary should not in time engross the whole land.

debates.question: Is a real division of land in view?

positions.position: No: neither the conquest, the return, the latter-day conversion nor a type of heaven fits; the allotment is the settling of Christ's kingdom through the world.
Not in the Jewish state; fulfilled in the Christian church, which was as new as this division is unlike the old.
Yes, on repossession, each family by its former allotment; but only the temple, priests and prince are provided for here, not the whole land.
Dividing by lot implies nothing of chance, since each tribe is later assigned its portion by name.

debates.question: In what unit are the twenty-five thousand measured?

positions.position: Reeds, as the English supplies: a hundred and fifty thousand cubits, over forty-seven statute miles.
Cubits, giving twelve miles and a half.

debates.question: What is the city of the oblation?

positions.position: Not Jerusalem: nothing identifies it, its position is different, and Jerusalem seems to have faded from the prophet's sight like the ark.
The capital and its citizens, large enough to receive the tribes.
The civil state of God's people under the spiritual reign.

outliers.claim: Mends a clause in the Levites' portion that he says admits of no satisfactory explanation as it stands, transposing two letters in one word and altering a letter in the next to read a possession of gates to dwell in, gates being an ordinary word for cities.

Rejects the suggestion that the priests' unusually large territory replaces the tithes this prophet never mentions, since the law of tithes was ancient and so large a change would not pass without a word; the enlargement is proportioned to the enlarged sanctuary instead.

9.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and spoil, and execute judgment and justice, take away your exactions from my people, saith the Lord God. Ye shall have just balances, and a just ephah, and a just bath. The ephah and the bath shall be of one measure, that the bath may contain the tenth part of an homer, and the ephah the tenth part of an homer: the measure thereof shall be after the homer. And the shekel shall be twenty gerahs: twenty shekels, five and twenty shekels, fifteen shekels, shall be your maneh. This is the oblation that ye shall offer; the sixth part of an ephah of an homer of wheat, and ye shall give the sixth part of an ephah of an homer of barley: Concerning the ordinance of oil, the bath of oil, ye shall offer the tenth part of a bath out of the cor, which is an homer of ten baths; for ten baths are an homer: And one lamb out of the flock, out of two hundred, out of the fat pastures of Israel; for a meat offering, and for a burnt offering, and for peace offerings, to make reconciliation for them, saith the Lord God. All the people of the land shall give this oblation for the prince in Israel. And it shall be the prince’s part to give burnt offerings, and meat offerings, and drink offerings, in the feasts, and in the new moons, and in the sabbaths, in all solemnities of the house of Israel: he shall prepare the sin offering, and the meat offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make reconciliation for the house of Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the measures historically -- the ephah early and apparently Egyptian, the bath much later and the largest liquid measure -- and shows how far their absolute value is from settled, one ancient historian giving the homer at eighty-six thousand gallons and the rabbis at forty-two thousand. He finds the clause about the maneh extremely obscure and its value unknown, and identifies the people's contribution as a regular tax to the prince, whose duty to furnish the festal sacrifices he calls an entirely new feature.

Gill makes the enforcement of true weights the civil magistrate's business, expects Christian princes content with ample salaries, and reads the small fractions -- a sixtieth, a hundredth, one lamb in two hundred -- as proof that the Mosaic dispensation is abrogated and as the measure of a moderate maintenance for Gospel ministers; the prince who provides the offerings he takes for the Messiah, refusing both the high priest and the civil ruler.

Clarke widens the charge against oppression to every ruler on earth, take away your exactions and abolish oppressive taxes, and reads the standardising of weights as a warning not to bring home the measures they had grown used to in captivity but to return to those prescribed to their forefathers.

Henry treats the verses as rules of distributive and commutative justice, on the ground that godliness without honesty is only a form of godliness, and turns the princes' excuse round: long custom is no defence, since no prescription justifies a wrong. On the weights he follows a contemporary computation, fixing the shekel and explaining the maneh's odd figures as three coins of twenty, twenty-five and fifteen shekels making one pound.

debates.question: What accounts for the maneh being twenty, twenty-five and fifteen shekels?

positions.position: The maneh was a hundred shekels as a weight but sixty as money; the three figures are coins of those weights making one pound.
The clause is extremely obscure and the maneh's value unknown; at most three different manehs may have been in use, but there is no other evidence.

debates.question: Who is the prince who provides the offerings?

positions.position: The Messiah, Prince and Priest together, whose one sacrifice answers all the many that typified it; neither the high priest nor the civil ruler.
The civil ruler, now bound by an entirely new duty to furnish from the people's tax what the older law had left to freewill offering.
The ruler, to whom the oblation is a present or offering.

debates.question: What do the small fractions of the contribution show?

positions.position: That the Mosaic dispensation is abrogated: not tithes of all things but a sixtieth, a hundredth and one lamb in two hundred, the measure of a moderate ministerial maintenance.
A regular tax to the prince, called a heave offering like the land, levied on the year's increase so that the sanctuary offerings can be furnished.

outliers.claim: Warns that the homer, which was ten ephahs, must be carefully distinguished from the omer, which was a tenth of one, the two words being quite different in Hebrew.
Reads the standardising of weights and measures as a warning against bringing home the standards the people had grown used to during the captivity.

18.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; In the first month, in the first day of the month, thou shalt take a young bullock without blemish, and cleanse the sanctuary: And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering, and put it upon the posts of the house, and upon the four corners of the settle of the altar, and upon the posts of the gate of the inner court. And so thou shalt do the seventh day of the month for every one that erreth, and for him that is simple: so shall ye reconcile the house. In the first month, in the fourteenth day of the month, ye shall have the passover, a feast of seven days; unleavened bread shall be eaten. And upon that day shall the prince prepare for himself and for all the people of the land a bullock for a sin offering. And seven days of the feast he shall prepare a burnt offering to the Lord, seven bullocks and seven rams without blemish daily the seven days; and a kid of the goats daily for a sin offering. And he shall prepare a meat offering of an ephah for a bullock, and an ephah for a ram, and an hin of oil for an ephah. In the seventh month, in the fifteenth day of the month, shall he do the like in the feast of the seven days, according to the sin offering, according to the burnt offering, and according to the meat offering, and according to the oil.

schools.summary: Ellicott catalogues the departures from the older law -- goats replaced by bullocks, a sin offering on a seventh day the law knows nothing of, the blood put on the posts and the settle instead of sprinkled on the altar's sides, richer passover offerings but a reduced and simplified autumn feast, and the outright omission of the Feast of Weeks, the Day of Atonement and the Day of Trumpets -- and argues that a priest could not have made such changes unknowingly, so the vision must be ideal. Keil and Delitzsch take the wording of the passover clause to mean the feast is kept as first appointed, with the evening meal.

Gill notes that the seventh-day rule is new and has no place in the law of Moses, citing a rabbi to the same effect, reads the blood of the sin offering as an emblem of the blood of Christ, and counts out the intervals between the cleansing of the sanctuary and the passover.

Clarke says flatly that there is nothing of this cleansing of the sanctuary in the law of Moses and takes it for a new and perhaps annual ceremony; he glosses the simple as one wanting understanding to conduct himself properly, and on the seventh-month feast observes only that the prince does exactly what he did at the passover.

debates.question: Is the sin offering of the seventh day for the sanctuary or for the people?

positions.position: For both: the day replaces the Day of Atonement, whose sacrifices were at once for the sins of priests and people and for the tabernacle, since the holy place needed purifying because of the sins of the people among whom it stood.
For those who err through want of understanding rather than wilfully.

debates.question: How do these sacrifices compare with those the law required?

positions.position: Much richer at the passover, a whole ephah going to each victim where the law asked graded portions; but at the autumn feast simplified and much reduced, with the eighth day dropped.
Identical between the two feasts: the prince offers the same victims with the same ceremonies at the second as at the first.

debates.question: Why does the ritual depart from the law of Moses?

positions.position: Because the changes are deliberate: a priest knew the law, so the departures, like those in the division of the land, mark the vision as ideal, and no attempt was ever made to carry them out.
The cleansing is simply a new ceremony, perhaps an annual purification.
The seventh-day rule is new and unknown to the law, as a rabbi also owns.

outliers.claim: Explains the absence of any name for the autumn feast by supposing that the custom of living in booths is to be discontinued, and observes that the whole scheme was regarded by the prophet's contemporaries and successors as purely ideal.
Finds in the wording of the passover clause the thought that the feast is to be kept in the manner first appointed, with the paschal meal in the evening.
